case_study_insert.main_stem: Harlow Valley Cooperative (HVC) is a cooperative in the confectionery sector, employing a workforce of 56. Founded in 2015 by chef Rowan Harlow, it makes organic chocolate bars for health-food shops and online customers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. HVC plans to invest $780,000 in a new moulding line with compostable wrappers, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $209,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.60 a unit and a selling price of $11.10, and currently produces 85,000 units a year. HVC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and wrapper waste at the moulding line has reached 6%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The moulding line produced 21,000 bars last month at a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 37 to 20 per month. Average delivery time is 3.0 days. A survey of 490 shoppers found that 69% preferred compostable wrappers and 54% would pay up to $0.40 more. A skills audit shows 16 of 56 staff need on-the-job training on the new moulder; off-the-job training at the local college costs $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harlow Valley Cooperative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs on HVC's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.25 to $14.10 per hour from April 2026, lifting the cooperative's wage bill. (3) Wholesale cocoa, sugar and wrapper costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, and confectionery inflation is 7.9%, while consumer spending on organic chocolate grew 3.4%.

questions.question_text: HVC plans to finance part of its moulding-line expansion with a $480,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for HVC of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs HVC no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while the cooperative services its other commitments and has committed $780,000 to the new moulding line. Every dollar not paid as interest can help absorb the 12.7% rise in cocoa, sugar and wrapper costs, allowing HVC to hold the $11.10 selling price for health-food shops and online buyers.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and default risk of a $480,000 bank loan, so the $300,000 can fund compostable wrappers without risking the moulder's repossession if demand for organic chocolate falls short of 85,000 units. It also keeps decision-making inside the cooperative and its 56 members, avoiding lender conditions on how the flat, democratic team operates, which suits HVC's member-owned structure and its $209,000 a year of fixed costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to HVC's costs, financing and ownership.

questions.question_text: HVC is relaunching its chocolate bars in compostable wrappers. Consider national television advertising, in-store health-food shop demonstrations, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HVC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would create fast awareness of the compostable-wrapper bars among all chocolate buyers. However, airtime is very expensive for a 56-member cooperative funding a $780,000 moulding line, and much of the mass audience does not shop in health-food stores, so the spend would be poorly targeted and difficult to afford.

In-store health-food shop demonstrations: Tastings let HVC show the compostable wrappers and the organic recipe directly to shoppers at the point of sale, supporting the 21,000 bars produced monthly and explaining the fall in defect rate to 2.9%. Drawbacks are high staff time, limited reach to a handful of shops, and dependence on shop permission, which cannot build national awareness quickly.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and ethical-living influencers can target exactly the 69% of 490 surveyed shoppers who prefer compostable wrappers and the 54% who would pay up to $0.40 more, showing the wrappers in short videos with measurable engagement and low cost per contact. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, but the segment fit is strongest and it reaches online customers nationally.

Recommendation: HVC should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the research-identified shoppers who value compostable wrappers, costs far less than television and scales beyond the few shops covered by demonstrations, while supporting the $11.10 price and online sales. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 56-member cooperative spending $780,000; in-store demonstrations are rejected as too labour-intensive and narrow, though a few can supplement the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to HVC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HVC's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in HVC's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and demonstrations.

questions.question_text: HVC's labour turnover is rising and wrapper waste has reached 6%. Explain two benefits for HVC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation and reduce waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HVC's 56 members a say in how the new moulder is run, raising job satisfaction and intrinsic motivation in a flat cooperative where members expect involvement. This can slow the rising labour turnover without hiring extra supervisors, keeping the trained workforce intact.

Point 2: Involving operators in decisions taps their practical knowledge of the moulder, generating ideas to cut the 6% wrapper waste and sustain the 2.9% defect rate. Greater commitment protects the 85,000-unit output and the $5.50 contribution per unit. The $700 off-the-job training budget can then be targeted at the 16 staff who still need skills, rather than spent on workers who are already disengaged.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to HVC's turnover, waste, defect rate and training.

questions.question_text: HVC must train 16 staff on the new moulder. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should HVC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the moulder is tailored to HVC's own machines and quality checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 16 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 21,000-bar monthly output and the improvement to a 2.9% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that trainers are working operators whose own output falls, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for health-food shop audits.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $700 per employee offers structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 16 staff, costing $11,200 — manageable against the $780,000 investment. However, it takes staff away from the line when wrapper waste is already 6%, reducing capacity, and generic content may not match HVC's moulder, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: HVC should choose on-the-job training first, then send a few senior operators for the college certificate. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids output loss while waste is 6% and turnover rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because $11,200 and sixteen absences would disrupt shop and online orders, and the course can be added once the moulder is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to HVC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in HVC's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in HVC's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HVC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 38,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 85,000-unit output; pricing against $209,000 fixed costs; loan affordability for the $780,000 moulder; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.06 to reduce 6% wrapper waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate answer in each calculation; 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $209,000 ÷ ($11.10 − $5.60) = $209,000 ÷ $5.50 = 38,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 38,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.10 − $5.60 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HVC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 38,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 85,000 units, a margin of safety of 47,000 units, to see how far organic-chocolate demand could fall before the new moulder loses money.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.50 lets HVC test a shop discount: a $0.40 cut would leave $5.10, showing the extra volume needed to cover $209,000 of fixed costs.
3. Knowing contribution and fixed costs helps check that 85,000 bars generate enough to service the $480,000 bank loan before the cooperative commits to the $780,000 moulder.
4. Unit cost of $8.06 ($209,000 ÷ 85,000 units + $5.60) gives a quarterly benchmark to isolate the 6% wrapper waste and 2.9% defect rate, guiding supplier talks amid 12.7% cocoa and wrapper inflation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HVC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HVC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $72,000 inventories + $120,000 trade receivables + $42,000 cash = $234,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $145,000 + $50,000 = $255,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $180,000 and $170,000 gives 1.30 and 1.50. Excluding inventories, $162,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.90 in 2024 and $195,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.15 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The broader measure rose from 1.30 to 1.50 as current liabilities fell from $180,000 to $170,000 and current assets grew to $255,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.90 to 1.15, helped by inventories falling from $72,000 to $60,000, so HVC can cover short-term debts without relying on selling chocolate stock — useful while it services a $480,000 bank loan and invests $780,000 in a moulder. However, trade receivables rose from $120,000 to $145,000, tying up cash that could fund the 6.4% wage rise; if health-food shops or online platforms pay late, the improvement could weaken.

Conclusion: HVC's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter measure now exceeds 1 without depending on inventories. The main risk is rising receivables, so the cooperative should tighten credit control before drawing further on the $480,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with some contextual analysis.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations plus detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HVC of using compostable wrappers for its chocolate bars.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Compostable wrappers match the 69% of 490 surveyed shoppers who prefer them and the 54% who would pay up to $0.40 more, helping HVC defend the $5.50 contribution per unit as cocoa, sugar and wrapper costs rise 12.7%. The positioning suits its organic brand and health-food shop and online customers, supporting the $780,000 moulder.

Disadvantage: Compostable film usually costs more than ordinary plastic, raising the $5.60 variable cost per unit unless the full $0.40 premium is secured across the range. If the wrappers seal poorly they could worsen the 6% wrapper waste and the 2.9% defect rate, adding cost to the 85,000-bar output just when labour turnover is rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using HVC's research, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 12.7% rise in input costs will affect HVC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): HVC has a $480,000 bank loan, and if it is variable-rate the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% × $480,000 = $3,600 (0.0075 × $480,000). That is small against $209,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan were fixed-rate the charge would be zero. Higher rates may make consumers more cautious about premium organic chocolate and raise future borrowing costs, but HVC can largely cap this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.10 per hour): HVC has a workforce of 56 in moulding and packing, so this raises its wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay rates are given, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible test is productivity — 85,000 units ÷ 56 staff is about 1,518 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $5.50 contribution.

Input cost inflation (12.7% cocoa, sugar and wrappers): The insert never decomposes the $5.60 variable cost, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 12.7% it would add 12.7% × $5.60 = $0.71 per unit, and at 85,000 units that is about $60,400 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution, and 7.9% confectionery inflation may limit HVC's ability to pass costs on to shops and online buyers.

Conclusion: The 12.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats on every one of the 85,000 bars and directly erodes the $5.50 contribution behind the $780,000 moulder, whereas the interest rise costs at most about $3,600 and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to HVC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HVC's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
